title: Levantine grammar
about: Only what is different from Standard Arabic, for someone who has done the Arabic grammar course: the sounds, the shorter endings, the everyday verb forms (b-, ʿam, raḥ), saying no, want, can and must, “there is”, “mine”, the numbers and linking your ideas. Everything that works as in Standard Arabic is left out. Every example is everyday Levantine as spoken in Damascus and Beirut, with Levantine vowel marks and a reading in Latin letters.

lessons.title: Sound like a Levantine speaker
lessons.summary: The few regular sound changes that turn the Standard words you know into Levantine ones: “a lot” is ktīr, “he said” is ʔāl.
lessons.topic: {{ق}} as a glottal stop, {{ث ذ ظ}} as t, d, ḍ, “ay” and “aw” as ē and ō, short vowels dropped

blocks.p: Levantine Arabic is the everyday Arabic of Syria, Lebanon, Jordan and Palestine. Most of its words are the Standard words you already know, **said differently**. Learn a few regular changes and you will recognise hundreds of words at once, and say them the way people do in Damascus and Beirut.

blocks.means: the everyday spoken Arabic of a region (Levantine, Egyptian, Gulf, Moroccan), as opposed to Modern Standard Arabic, the written standard that every Arab learns at school.

table: ʔ, a catch in the throat (the break in “uh-oh”)
t (in a few learned words s)
d (in a few learned words z)
ḍ (in a few learned words z)

blocks.p: **Short vowels drop.** A short vowel in an open syllable often disappears, so many words start with two consonants: {{كْبِير|kbīr}} “big”, {{مْنِيح|mnīḥ}} “good”, {{كْتَاب|ktāb}} “book”. The ending {{ة}} is said -e, or -a after letters like ḥ, ʿ, ṣ, ṭ, r: {{شَغْلِة|shaghle}} “thing”, {{سَيَّارَة|sayyāra}} “car”.

blocks.tip: In Damascus and Beirut {{ق}} is almost always ʔ. In villages, and often in Jordan and Palestine, you will hear g ({{قَال|gāl}}) or even k. A few learned words keep q: {{القُرْآن|il-qurʔān}}, {{ثَقَافِة|thaqāfe}} “culture”.

mistakes.why: In everyday words {{ث}} is said t, and the first vowel drops: {{كْتِير|ktīr}}. With th it sounds like reading a newspaper aloud.
{{ذ}} becomes d, and Levantine writes it with {{د}}: {{هَادَا|hāda}}.

practice.q: How does someone from Damascus say {{قَال}} “he said”?
practice.why: In the cities {{ق}} is a glottal stop: ʔāl.
“ay” becomes ē in the cities: bēt. In the same way {{يَوْم}} “day” is yōm.

practice.q: How do you say “a lot” in Levantine?
Your turn: say a short sentence with one {{ق}} word and one {{ث}} word, the Levantine way.

answers.tr: There's no time.
There's a lot of snow.

lessons.title: Drop the endings: two of a thing, and plurals
lessons.summary: Say “two new books” and “the girls went” without case endings, the dual or feminine plurals.
lessons.topic: No case endings or tanwīn; the dual {{ـَيْن}} on nouns only; one plural for men and women

blocks.p: **No case endings.** Levantine never says the -u, -a, -i at the end of a word, nor -un, -an, -in: {{البَيْت كْبِير|il-bēt kbīr}} where Standard Arabic has {{البَيْتُ كَبِيرٌ}}. Word order, not endings, shows who does what.

**The dual lives on in nouns only.** Add {{ـَيْن|-ēn}} to a noun for “two”: {{كْتَابَيْن|ktābēn}} “two books”, {{سَنْتَيْن|santēn}} “two years”, {{يَوْمَيْن|yōmēn}} “two days”. Adjectives, verbs and pronouns take the plural: {{كْتَابَيْن جْدَاد|ktābēn jdād}} “two new books”.
**One plural for everyone.** There are no feminine plural verbs, adjectives or pronouns: men or women, it's {{هِنِّ|hinne}} “they”, {{إِنْتُو|intu}} “you all”, {{رَاحُوا|rāḥu}} “they went”.

ex.tr: I stayed in Damascus for two months.

blocks.tip: With most nouns people simply say {{تْنَيْن|tnēn}} “two” + the plural: {{تْنَيْن رْفْقَات|tnēn rfaʔāt}} “two friends”. {{ـَيْن}} is commonest with time words: {{يَوْمَيْن، شَهْرَيْن، سَنْتَيْن}}.

mistakes.why: Levantine has no feminine plural verb: men or women, it's {{رَاحُوا}}.
Only the noun takes the dual ending {{ـَيْن}}; the adjective is plural, and there are no case endings.

practice.tr: I lived in Beirut for two years.
practice.why: Two of a time word: {{ـَيْن}}, with no case ending.

practice.q: “They went”, said about a group of women, is…
Your turn: say how long you stayed somewhere, or how long ago something happened, with {{يَوْمَيْن}}, {{شَهْرَيْن}} or {{سَنْتَيْن}}.

answers.tr: I stayed in Lebanon for two days.
I bought the car two years ago.

lessons.title: Say I, you, he, she: pronouns and “my, his, her”
lessons.summary: The Levantine pronouns, and the endings for “my, your, his, her”: bētu “his house”.
lessons.topic: {{أَنَا، إِنْتَ، إِنْتِ، هُوِّ، هِيِّ، نِحْنَا، إِنْتُو، هِنِّ}}; the endings {{ـُو، ـْها، ـْكُن، ـْهُن}}

goal.tr: He's my friend, and this is his house.

blocks.p: The pronouns are close to Standard Arabic; the changes are in the vowels and in the plurals, which are the same for men and women.
**My, your, his.** The endings work as in Standard Arabic, but “his” is {{ـُو|-u}} and “her” is {{ـْها|-a}}, with the h hardly heard: {{بَيْتُو|bētu}} “his house”, {{بَيْتْها|bēta}} “her house”.

dialog.tr: That's my brother, and that's his wife.

blocks.tip: After a long vowel “his” is a light h: {{أَخُوه|akhūh}} “his brother”, {{أَبُوه|abūh}} “his father”.

mistakes.why: “His” is {{ـُو}} in Levantine; {{ـُهُ}} is Standard.
One “they” for men and women: {{هِنِّ}}.

practice.tr: This is his house, he lives here.

lines.tr: Hi! And where are you (two) from?

practice.q: Your turn: introduce someone in your family: who it is, and his or her name.

answers.tr: This is my brother, his name is Sami.
This is my sister, her name is Lina.

lessons.title: Point at things: this, that, these
lessons.summary: Say “this house”, “that girl”, “these are my friends”, and the Lebanese hayda.
lessons.topic: {{هَادَا، هَاي، هَدُول، هَدَاك، هَدِيك}}; Lebanese {{هَيْدَا، هَيْدِي، هَيْدُول}}; {{هالْـ}} “this” before a noun

goal.tr: I want this one, not that one.

blocks.p: Standard {{هَذَا، هَذِهِ، هَؤُلَاءِ، ذَلِكَ، تِلْكَ}} become:

**Before a noun**, “this” is usually just {{هالْـ|hal-}} joined to the noun in place of its “the”: {{هالبَيْت|hal-bēt}} “this house”, {{هالبِنْت|hal-bint}} “this girl”. You can also put the full word before the noun with its {{الْـ}}: {{هَادَا البَيْت|hāda l-bēt}}. “That” always comes before the noun: {{هَدَاك البَيْت|hadāk il-bēt}} “that house”.

ex.tr: This is the best restaurant in Beirut.

blocks.tip: {{هالْـ}} also means “so, such”: {{هالقَدّ|hal-ʔadd}} “this much, so much”, {{هالأَيَّام|hal-ayyām}} “these days”.

mistakes.why: In speech {{هَذَا}} is {{هَادَا}}, and before a noun people usually say {{هالْـ}}.
“That” comes before the noun.

practice.q: How do you say “these are my friends”?
Your turn: point at two things near you and say something about them, with {{هالْـ}} and {{هَدَاك}} or {{هَدِيك}}.

answers.tr: This book is new, and that one's old.
This glass is mine, and that one's yours.

lessons.title: Ask what, where, when, why and how
lessons.summary: The Levantine question words: shū, wēn, ēmta, lēsh, kīf, mīn, ʔaddēsh.
lessons.topic: {{شُو، وَيْن، إِيمْتَى، لَيْش، كِيف، شْلُون، مِين، قَدِّيش، مْنِين}}

goal.tr: What's your name, and where are you from?

blocks.p: A question keeps the order of the answer: the question word can come first, or stay where the answer would be: {{شُو بِدَّك؟|shū biddak?}} or {{بِدَّك شُو؟|biddak shū?}} “What do you want?”. A yes-or-no question is just the sentence said with a rising voice: {{إِنْتَ مِن هَوْن؟|inta min hōn?}} “Are you from here?”
Question words take the person endings too: {{وَيْنَك؟|wēnak?}} “Where are you?”, {{كِيفِك؟|kīfik?}} “How are you?” (to a woman).

ex.tr: How are you? How's your health?

dialog.tr: From Canada. How much is the fare?

mistakes.why: {{مَاذَا}} and {{تُرِيدُ}} are Standard; in speech it's {{شُو بِدَّك}}.
“Where” is {{وَيْن}}, and it can take the person's ending: {{وَيْنَك}}.

practice.q: At the market: choose your replies.
How do you say “when will you come back?”
Your turn: ask someone new three questions.

answers.tr: What's your name? Where do you live?
Where are you from? And why did you come to Damascus?

lessons.title: Say what you do: the b- present
lessons.summary: Put b- on the present for what you do, usually or in general: bishrab ʔahwe kill yōm “I drink coffee every day”.
lessons.topic: The present with {{بِـ}}: {{بِكْتُب، بْتِكْتُب، بْيِكْتُب، مْنِكْتُب}}; without it after {{بِدّ}}, {{لَازِم}}, {{رَح}}

goal.t: بِشْتِغِل كِلّ يَوْم لَحَدّ السَّاعَة خَمْسِة.
goal.r: bishtighil kill yōm la-ḥadd is-sāʿa khamse.
goal.tr: I work every day until five.

blocks.p: Standard {{يَكْتُبُ}} “he writes” has one form. Levantine has two. With {{بِـ|b-}} the present says what you do, usually or in general: {{بِكْتُب|biktub}} “I write”. Without it, the **plain present** follows words like “want”, “must” and “will”: {{بِدِّي إِكْتُب|biddi iktub}} “I want to write”.

blocks.means: the Levantine present without {{بِـ}}: {{يِكْتُب|yiktub}}. It follows {{بِدِّي}} “I want”, {{لَازِم}} “must”, {{رَح}} “will” and {{عَم}} “-ing”, and it gives orders with {{لَا}}: {{لَا تْرُوح|lā trūḥ}} “don't go”.

blocks.p: Notice that “we” takes {{مْـ|m-}} in place of {{بْـ}}: {{مْنِحْكِي|mniḥki}} “we talk”. And the endings follow the last unit: {{ـُوا|-u}} for any group, men or women.

ex.tr: I want to drink some water.

blocks.tip: In fast speech {{بْيِـ}} often sounds like {{بِيـ}}: {{بِيِكْتُب}} and {{بْيِكْتُب}} are the same word, written either way.

mistakes.tr: I want to drink some water.
mistakes.why: After {{بِدِّي}} the verb is plain, without {{بِـ}}.
“We” takes {{مْـ}}, not {{بْـ}}.

practice.why: Something you do every day: {{بِـ}}, and “I” is {{بِـ}}.
“We” takes {{مْـ}}; {{نِشْتِغِل}} alone is the plain present.

practice.q: How do you say “do you speak Arabic?”
Your turn: say three things you do every day.

answers.tr: I get up early and drink coffee.
I go to work by bus.

lessons.title: Say what you're doing now: ʿam
lessons.summary: Put ʿam before the verb for “-ing”: ʿam iḥki “I'm talking”.
lessons.topic: {{عَم}} + the present: what is happening now, and how long it has been going on

blocks.p: Standard Arabic uses the same present for “I write” and “I'm writing”. Levantine marks “-ing” with {{عَم|ʿam}}: {{عَم إِكْتُب|ʿam iktub}} “I'm writing (right now)”. After {{عَم}} the verb is usually plain; in Lebanon you will also hear it with {{بِـ}}: {{عَم بِكْتُب|ʿam biktub}}.
With {{مِن|min}} “for, since”, {{عَم}} says how long something has been going on: {{عَم إِسْتَنَّاك مِن سَاعَة|ʿam istannāk min sāʿa}} “I've been waiting for you for an hour”.

ex.tr: I've been learning Arabic for a year.
I don't understand what you're saying.

dialog.tr: Where are you? What are you doing?
I'm in the car, I'm driving.

dialog.t: طَيِّب، لَا تِحْكِي وْإِنْتَ عَم تْسُوق!
dialog.r: ṭayyib, lā tiḥki w-inta ʿam tsūʔ!
dialog.tr: OK, don't talk while you're driving!

mistakes.why: For something happening now, put {{عَم}} before the verb.
{{عَم}} goes with verbs of doing, not with {{بِدِّي}} “I want”.

options: I've been waiting for you for an hour
I'll wait for you for an hour
I waited for you an hour ago
practice.why: {{عَم}} + {{مِن}}: still going on, and since when.

practice.q: A phone call: choose your replies.
How do you say “what are you doing now?”
Your turn: say what you and two other people are doing right now.

answers.t: أَنَا عَم إِدْرُس، وْأُخْتِي عَم تِنَام.
answers.r: ana ʿam idrus, w-ukhti ʿam tnām.
answers.tr: I'm studying, and my sister is sleeping.

answers.t: إِمِّي عَم تِطْبُخ، وْبَيِّي عَم يِقْرَا الجَرِيدِة.
answers.r: immi ʿam tiṭbukh, w-bayyi ʿam yiʔra l-jarīde.
answers.tr: My mum's cooking, and my dad's reading the paper.

lessons.title: Talk about the future: raḥ
lessons.summary: Put raḥ before the plain present: raḥ nrūḥ bukra “we'll go tomorrow”.

goal.tr: We're going to the sea tomorrow.

blocks.p: Standard {{سَوْفَ}} and {{سَـ}} are never heard. Levantine puts {{رَح|raḥ}} before the plain present, without {{بِـ}}: {{رَح إِحْكِي مَعُو|raḥ iḥki maʿo}} “I'll talk to him”. In fast speech it shrinks to {{حَـ|ḥa-}}: {{حَنْرُوح|ḥa-nrūḥ}} “we'll go”.
“Won't” is {{مَا رَح|mā raḥ}}: {{مَا رَح إِقْدَر إِجِي|mā raḥ iʔdar iji}} “I won't be able to come”.

ex.tr: He won't make it in time.

blocks.tip: {{رَح}} never changes for the person: {{رَح إِجِي|raḥ iji}} “I'll come”, {{رَح يِجُوا|raḥ yiju}} “they'll come”. The verb after it does.

mistakes.why: After {{رَح}} the verb is plain, without {{بِـ}}.
{{سَوْفَ}} belongs to written Standard Arabic.

practice.tr: We're going to go out tonight.

practice.q: How do you say “I'll call you tomorrow”?
Your turn: say three things you're going to do this weekend.

answers.t: رَح زُور تِيتَا، وْرَح نَام مْنِيح.
answers.r: raḥ zūr tēta, w-raḥ nām mnīḥ.
answers.tr: I'm going to visit grandma, and I'm going to sleep well.
We're going up to the village with my friends.

lessons.title: Tell what happened: the past
lessons.summary: The past the Levantine way: shift “I saw”, rāḥu “they went”, katbit “she wrote”.
lessons.topic: Past endings {{ـْت، ـْتِي، ـِت، ـْنَا، ـْتُوا، ـُوا}}; i for a: {{شِرِب، فِهِم}}

goal.tr: Yesterday I saw my friend at the market.

blocks.p: The past works as in Standard Arabic, with endings on the verb, but the endings are shorter and have no final vowels.

So {{كَتَبْت}} is both “I wrote” and “you wrote”: the situation, or {{أَنَا}} and {{إِنْتَ}}, says which. Many verbs have i where Standard has a: {{شِرِب|shirib}} “he drank”, {{فِهِم|fihim}} “he understood”, {{عِمِل|ʿimil}} “he did”. Hollow verbs shorten as in Standard Arabic: {{رَاح|rāḥ}} “he went”, {{رِحْت|riḥt}} “I went”.

ex.tr: What did you all do yesterday?
My sister got married last year.

mistakes.why: No vowel after the ending: {{ـْت}}.
“She” ends in {{ـِت|-it}}, and the vowel before it drops: {{كَتْبِت}}.

practice.tr: Yesterday we went to the market.
I went yesterday, and I'll go tomorrow.

practice.q: How do you say “we had coffee and talked”?
Your turn: tell what you did yesterday, in two or three sentences.

answers.tr: Yesterday I got up early and went to work.
In the evening we watched a film and ate pizza.

lessons.title: Say no: mā, mū and mish
lessons.summary: mā for verbs; mū (Syria) or mish (Lebanon, Palestine) for everything else; lā for “don't!”.
lessons.topic: {{مَا}} + verb; {{مُو}} / {{مِش}} + noun, adjective, place, participle; {{لَا}} + plain present

goal.t: مَا بَعْرِف، أَنَا مُو مِن هَوْن.
goal.r: mā baʿrif, ana mū min hōn.
goal.tr: I don't know, I'm not from here.

blocks.p: Standard Arabic has {{لَا، لَمْ، لَنْ، لَيْسَ}}. Levantine needs two words. **{{مَا|mā}}** goes before any verb, past, present or future: {{مَا بَعْرِف|mā baʿrif}} “I don't know”, {{مَا شِفْتُو|mā shiftu}} “I didn't see him”, {{مَا رَح إِجِي|mā raḥ iji}} “I won't come”.

**{{مُو|mū}}** (Damascus) or **{{مِش|mish}}** (Lebanon, Palestine, Jordan) goes before anything that isn't a verb: a noun, an adjective, a place, or a participle like {{فَاهِم|fāhim}} “understanding”: {{مُو مْنِيح|mū mnīḥ}} “not good”, {{مِش فَاهِم|mish fāhim}} “I don't get it”.

**Don't!** is {{لَا|lā}} + the plain present: {{لَا تْرُوح|lā trūḥ}} “don't go”, {{لَا تْعَصِّب|lā tʿaṣṣib}} “don't get angry”. In Palestine and Jordan you will also hear {{ـِش|-ish}} on the end of the verb: {{مَا بَعْرِفِش|mā baʿrifish}} “I don't know”.

mistakes.why: {{عِنْدِي}} “I have” works like a verb: it takes {{مَا}}.
An adjective takes {{مُو}} or {{مِش}}.
A verb takes {{مَا}}.

practice.tr: I don't know where he lives.

practice.why: An order not to do something: {{لَا}} + the plain present.

practice.q: How do you say “I'm not from here”?
Your turn: say something you don't like, something you didn't do yesterday, and something you're not.

answers.t: مَا بْحِبّ الشِّتِي، وْمْبَارِح مَا طْلِعْت.
answers.r: mā bḥibb ish-shiti, w-mbāreḥ mā ṭliʿt.
answers.tr: I don't like the rain, and yesterday I didn't go out.

answers.t: أَنَا مُو تَعْبَان، بَسّ مَا نِمْت مْنِيح.
answers.r: ana mū taʿbān, bass mā nimt mnīḥ.
answers.tr: I'm not tired, but I didn't sleep well.

lessons.title: Say what you want, can and must
lessons.summary: biddi “I want”, fīni “I can”, lāzim “I have to”, each followed by the plain present.

goal.t: بِدِّي رُوح، بَسّ لَازِم خَلِّص شُغْلِي.
goal.r: biddi rūḥ, bass lāzim khalliṣ shughli.
goal.tr: I want to go, but I have to finish my work.

blocks.p: **Want** is {{بِدّ|bidd}} with the possessive endings, then the plain present, with no {{أَنْ}}: {{بِدِّي رُوح|biddi rūḥ}} “I want to go”. It isn't a verb, so “I wanted” is {{كَان بِدِّي|kān biddi}}, and “I don't want” is {{مَا بِدِّي|mā biddi}}.

**Can** is {{فِي|fī}} with the same endings: {{فِينِي|fīni}} “I can”, {{فِيك|fīk}} “you can” (Palestine, Jordan: {{بَقْدَر|baʔdar}}). **Must, have to** is {{لَازِم|lāzim}}, the same for everyone: {{لَازِم رُوح|lāzim rūḥ}} “I have to go”, {{لَازِم تْرُوح|lāzim trūḥ}} “you have to go”.

ex.tr: Do you want coffee or tea?
You have to drink a lot of water.

mistakes.why: {{أُرِيدُ أَنْ}} is Standard; in speech it's {{بِدِّي}}, with no {{أَنْ}}.
After {{بِدّ}}, the plain present.
{{بِدّ}} isn't a verb; its past is {{كَان بِدِّي}}.

practice.q: At the café: choose your replies.
How do you say “do you want coffee or tea?”
Your turn: say something you want to do, something you can't do, and something you have to do this week.

answers.t: بِدِّي رُوح عَالبَحِر، بَسّ مَا فِينِي.
answers.r: biddi rūḥ ʿal-baḥer, bass mā fīni.
answers.tr: I want to go to the sea, but I can't.
I have to finish the work before Friday.

lessons.title: Say there is, and there isn't
lessons.summary: fī “there is”, mā fī “there isn't”, kān fī “there was”.

goal.tr: Is there a good restaurant here?

blocks.p: Standard says {{هُنَاكَ}} or {{يُوجَدُ}}. Levantine just says {{فِي|fī}}, the word for “in”: {{فِي مُشْكِلِة|fī mushkle}} “there's a problem”. With {{مَا}} it is “there isn't”, and {{مَا فِي}} on its own answers “no, there isn't any”.

Past and future go through {{كَان}}: {{كَان فِي عَجْقَة|kān fī ʿajʔa}} “there was a traffic jam”, {{رَح يْكُون فِي حَفْلِة|raḥ ykūn fī ḥafle}} “there's going to be a party”. In Palestine you will hear {{فِيش|fīsh}} for “there isn't”.

ex.tr: There's no money in the bank.
There were lots of people at the wedding.
Is there any sugar? — No, there isn't any.
There's going to be rain tomorrow.

mistakes.why: In speech, {{فِي}}.
{{فِي}} is said no with {{مَا}}.

practice.tr: There were a lot of people yesterday.
There's no time, we have to go.

practice.q: How do you say “there's someone at the door”?
Your turn: say what there is and isn't in your street.

answers.t: بِشَارِعْنَا فِي فُرْن، بَسّ مَا فِي صَيْدَلِيِّة.
answers.r: b-shāriʿna fī furn, bass mā fī ṣaydaliyye.
answers.tr: In our street there's a bakery, but there's no pharmacy.

answers.t: فِي جْنَيْنِة زْغِيرِة وْكَان فِي سِينَمَا.
answers.r: fī jnēne zghīre w-kān fī sīnama.
answers.tr: There's a small park, and there used to be a cinema.

lessons.title: Say mine and yours: tabaʿ
lessons.summary: is-sayyāra tabaʿi “my car”, tabaʿak “yours”: the everyday way to say whose.
lessons.topic: {{تَبَع}} + endings after a noun with {{الْـ}}; {{تَبَع مِين؟}} “whose?”

goal.tr: This bag is mine, not yours.

blocks.p: You can still say {{بَيْتِي|bēti}} “my house”, with the ending, as in Standard Arabic. But speakers often put **{{تَبَع|tabaʿ}}** “belonging to” after a noun with {{الْـ}}: {{البَيْت تَبَعِي|il-bēt tabaʿi}} “my house”. It is the usual way with long words and foreign words: {{المُوبَايِل تَبَعِي|il-mobāyl tabaʿi}} “my phone”.

On its own it means “mine, yours”: {{هَادَا تَبَعَك؟|hāda tabaʿak?}} “Is this yours?” Many say {{تَبَعِت|tabaʿit}} after a feminine noun and {{تَبَعُون|tabaʿūn}} after a plural; plain {{تَبَع}} is always right too.

ex.tr: Our house is near the sea.
It's not mine, it's my sister's.

mistakes.why: {{تَبَع}} comes after the noun.
The noun before {{تَبَع}} has {{الْـ}}.

practice.why: The noun, then {{تَبَع مِين}}. {{مِين هالكْتَاب}} would be “who is this book”.

practice.q: How do you say “where are my keys?”
Your turn: say whose two or three things near you are.

answers.tr: The phone is mine, and the book is my brother's.
Is this glass yours?

lessons.title: Count: the Levantine numbers
lessons.summary: One to twenty the Levantine way, tlāte and ḥdaʿsh, and how a noun follows a number.
lessons.topic: {{وَاحَد … عَشْرَة}}; short forms before a noun; 11 to 19 in {{ـطَعْش}}; a singular noun after 11

goal.tr: I have three boys and a girl.

blocks.p: The numbers are the Standard ones said the Levantine way ({{ث}} as t, no case endings), and they don't swap gender the way Standard numbers do. From 3 to 10 there is a short form before a noun.

**11 to 19** end in {{ـطَعْش|-ṭaʿsh}}: {{حْدَعْش|ḥdaʿsh}} 11, {{تْنَعْش|tnaʿsh}} 12, {{تْلَتَّعْش|tlattaʿsh}} 13, {{أَرْبَعْطَعْش|arbaʿṭaʿsh}} 14, {{خَمِسْطَعْش|khamisṭaʿsh}} 15, {{سِتَّعْش|sittaʿsh}} 16, {{سَبَعْطَعْش|sabaʿṭaʿsh}} 17, {{تْمَنْطَعْش|tmanṭaʿsh}} 18, {{تِسَعْطَعْش|tisaʿṭaʿsh}} 19. From 11 on, the noun is singular: {{حْدَعْش سَنِة|ḥdaʿsh sane}} “eleven years”, {{عِشْرِين لِيرَة|ʿishrīn līra}} “twenty lira”.

ex.tr: I'd like three kilos of tomatoes.

mistakes.why: The short form {{تْلَات}} before a noun, said with t.
From 11 on, the noun is singular.

practice.tr: I have three brothers and sisters.
practice.why: Before a noun, the short form.
After 11 and up, the noun is singular.

practice.tr: There are three rooms in the house.

practice.q: Your turn: say how old you are and how many people there are in your family.

answers.tr: I'm thirty.

answers.t: نِحْنَا خَمْسِة بِالعِيلِة: أَنَا، إِمِّي، بَيِّي، وْأُخْتَيْن.
answers.r: niḥna khamse bil-ʿēle: ana, immi, bayyi, w-ukhtēn.
answers.tr: There are five of us in the family: me, my mum, my dad and two sisters.

lessons.title: Say if and when: iza, law, lamma
lessons.summary: iza for real possibilities, law for imagined ones, lamma for “when”.
lessons.topic: {{إِزَا}} + past or present; {{لَوْ}} with {{كَان}}; {{لَمَّا}} “when” in statements

goal.tr: If you go, I'll go with you.

blocks.p: Standard {{إِذَا}} is said {{إِزَا|iza}}. The verb after it can be past or present with the same meaning: {{إِزَا إِجِيت|iza jīt}} or {{إِزَا بْتِجِي|iza btiji}} “if you come”. The result is an ordinary present or {{رَح}}, never {{سَـ}}: {{إِزَا إِجِيت، مْنِطْلَع سَوَا|iza jīt, mniṭlaʿ sawa}} “if you come, we'll go out together”.

For something imagined or impossible use **{{لَوْ|law}}** with {{كَان}}: {{لَوْ مَعِي مَصَارِي، كِنْت اشْتَرَيْت بَيْت|law maʿi maṣāri, kint shtarēt bēt}} “if I had money, I'd buy a house”. **{{لَمَّا|lamma}}** is “when” in a statement: {{لَمَّا وْصِلْت، كَانُوا نَايْمِين|lamma wṣilt, kānu nāymīn}} “when I arrived, they were asleep”.

ex.tr: If you like, you can come with us.
If it rains, we won't go out.

ex.t: لَوْ كِنْت مَطْرَحَك، مَا كِنْت حْكِيت.
ex.r: law kint maṭraḥak, mā kint ḥkīt.
ex.tr: If I were you, I wouldn't have said anything.

ex.t: لَمَّا كِنْت زْغِير، كِنْت سَاكِن بْحَلَب.
ex.r: lamma kint zghīr, kint sākin b-Ḥalab.
ex.tr: When I was little, I lived in Aleppo.

mistakes.why: No {{سَـ}}: the result is an ordinary present, or {{رَح}}.

mistakes.tr: When I arrived, they were asleep.
mistakes.why: {{إِيمْتَى}} only asks “when?”; in a statement it's {{لَمَّا}}.

practice.tr: If you want, you can come.
When I arrived, I called you.

practice.q: Which one imagines something (“if I had…”)?

practice.tr: If it rains, we won't go out.

practice.q: How do you say “if you go, I'll go with you”?
Your turn: what will you do if it's sunny this weekend? And what would you do if you had a month off?

answers.t: إِزَا كَان الطَّقْس حِلُو، رَح رُوح عَالبَحِر.
answers.r: iza kān iṭ-ṭaʔs ḥilu, raḥ rūḥ ʿal-baḥer.
answers.tr: If the weather's nice, I'll go to the sea.

answers.t: لَوْ عِنْدِي شَهِر عُطْلِة، كِنْت سَافَرْت عَلِبْنَان.
answers.r: law ʿindi shahr ʿuṭle, kint sāfart ʿa-libnān.
answers.tr: If I had a month off, I'd travel to Lebanon.

lessons.title: Connect your ideas: illi, innu, laʔinnu
lessons.summary: One word for who, which and that (illi), innu “that”, laʔinnu “because”, and mishān “so that”.
lessons.topic: {{اللِّي}} for every relative; {{إِنُّو}} + endings; {{لَإِنُّو}}; {{مِشَان}} + plain present

goal.tr: The girl you saw yesterday is my sister.

blocks.p: Standard {{الَّذِي، الَّتِي، الَّذِينَ}} are all **{{اللِّي|illi}}** in speech: {{الزَّلَمِة اللِّي سَاكِن جَنْبْنَا|iz-zalame illi sākin janbna}} “the man who lives next to us”. As in Standard Arabic, the verb after it repeats the noun as an ending: {{البِنْت اللِّي شِفْتها|il-bint illi shiftha}} “the girl (that) you saw (her)”.

**{{إِنُّو|innu}}** is “that” after say, know, think: {{بَعْرِف إِنُّو تَعْبَان|baʿrif innu taʿbān}} “I know (that) he's tired”. It takes the person endings like Standard {{أَنَّ}}: {{إِنَّك|innak}} “that you”, {{إِنِّي|inni}} “that I”. **{{لَإِنُّو|laʔinnu}}** is “because”, and **{{مِشَان|mishān}}** + the plain present is “so that, in order to”: {{جِيت مِشَان شُوفَك|jīt mishān shūfak}} “I came to see you”.

ex.tr: That's the man who helped me.

ex.t: مَا نِمْت مْنِيح لَإِنُّو كَان فِي شُوب.
ex.r: mā nimt mnīḥ laʔinnu kān fī shōb.
ex.tr: I didn't sleep well because it was hot.

ex.t: عَم إِتْعَلَّم عَرَبِي مِشَان إِحْكِي مَع جِيرَانِي.
ex.r: ʿam itʿallam ʿarabi mishān iḥki maʿ jīrāni.
ex.tr: I'm learning Arabic so I can talk to my neighbours.

blocks.tip: {{بَسّ|bass}} “but” and {{هَيْك|hēk}} “so, like this” glue a story together: {{تْأَخَّرْت، بَسّ وْصِلْت، وْهَيْك…|tʔakhkhart, bass wṣilt, w-hēk…}} “I was late, but I got there, and so…”

mistakes.why: In speech every “who, which, that” is {{اللِّي}}.
Standard {{أَنَّ}} is {{إِنُّو}} in speech, with the same endings: {{إِنَّك}} “that you”.

practice.tr: This is the book (that) I read.
I didn't go to work because I was ill.

options: I came because I saw you
I saw you when I came

practice.tr: I want the one you bought.

practice.q: How do you say “he said he'd be late”?
Your turn: why are you learning Levantine? Use {{لَإِنُّو}} or {{مِشَان}}.

answers.t: عَم إِتْعَلَّم شَامِي لَإِنُّو مَرْتِي مِن الشَّام.
answers.r: ʿam itʿallam shāmi laʔinnu marti min ish-shām.
answers.tr: I'm learning Levantine because my wife is from Damascus.

answers.t: بِدِّي إِتْعَلَّم مِشَان إِفْهَم الأَفْلَام وْالمُسَلْسَلَات.
answers.r: biddi itʿallam mishān ifham il-aflām w-il-musalsalāt.
answers.tr: I want to learn so I can understand films and TV series.
